I think that this maybe even is a bit too trivial... but for a clash it could be working because you might even be able to one-line it in some languages :D

Submitting as clash because the solution's really trivial, but I really have no problem whatsoever with it moving to Puzzles if it's deemed to complex a statement for clashing. (Sorry, no clashing in a long time on my side, I might be out of touch)

Please be careful if you edit: I've put a few ZERO WIDTH NON-JOINERs around to help general appearance.
I edited the "x2" case, the first empty line was wrong.

My forecast is that it's going to be *very* dependent on who reads it. Some are going to panic at the very sight of "Rubik", others are going to recognize it for the trivial problem it is.

The more general point is: it's the easiest in the series, but it has its place. It's doable in clash (hence my submitting it there), but it could actually make sense to duplicate it to community puzzles once the others "can it be solved this way" are approved, to enable a more gradual difficulty slope.

My proposed sample solution is 78 characters (though I'll admit I didn't spend as much on it as I would have on a clash). How long is yours? :D
i've taken the liberty to fix the missing space in last test case

Thanks for the report, thanks for solving.
I think it's fine in reverse; moreover it's been there long enough that if clashers thought it weren't, it would have been autoremoved from this mode by now.

To elaborate on the reverse mode: this is subjective, but in my opinion (1) it might not be clear that this is a rubik's cube, (2) there is pretty much no way to figure out that the cube is being solved using the "Restickering™ method" in reverse mode. Moreover, I don't think anyone will assume that it is the case without having access to the statement. So most reverse solutions likely just assume that only a smaller subset of checks is required for this specific problem, like checking the number of stickers, maybe checking the central faces have unique stickers, maybe checking that all the unique pieces of a rubik's cube are in place (like 8 correct corner pieces, 12 edge ones and again 6 face ones), etc. That is, there are a lot of checks one might want to / assume they need to implement. The only cases where Restickering solves the cube but the cube itself is unsolvable using normal methods are (I assume) ones with an edge flip or a corner twist, but they are quite a bit further down in the available tests and are hardly noticeable, and even if one notices it, there is no indication that "solvability" is determined by the Restickering; instead one might assume we just allow edge flips / corner twists --- and that is even if we assume one knows what edge flips / corner twists are (and I wouldn't assume those to be common knowledge)

P.S. thanks for answering :)

All you write is correct, but I still don't see the case against reverse.
It works, if only because little else could in clash time, also because a flip (that's possible to detect by eye) is there as SOLVABLE.

It might not be clear that this is a Rubik's cube, but that's irrelevant: you can still “IQ test” your way out from the cases by noticing letter balance is all that counts. This would not work for the latter instances in the series, e.g. take-apart-and-rebuild or however it's named, but those aren't available as clash.

I'd argue that while it is possible to see the flip, it's not at all noticeable. And if you do notice, it doesn't make it clear what "solvable" means. (restickering is _not_ an intuitive method to "solve" the cube)

The letter balance also is in no way detectable from just looking at the test cases -- this is a text representation, and differentiating between letters is quite hard when they are all mixed together; and while the first couple test cases are easy to see a difference, since same letters are grouped together, I'd say it's impossible to see how many of each letter there is for the other cases.

> if only because little else could in clash time

I'd say it is possible (even if on the harder side) to check for (1) "take it apart" consistency (2) or even edge-flip / corner-twist / center swap consistency in 15 minutes. It might be a bit messy / close to the time limit, but not anywhere close to long enough / difficult enough that it would be immediately obvious that it's not expected to be implemented.

IMO those checks are much more intuitive if you know about edge flips and such than the "restickering" method. In reverse mode it's not going to be clear that it's not what is expected.

> I'd argue that while it is possible to see the flip, it's not at all noticeable. And if you do notice, it doesn't make it clear what "solvable" means. (restickering is _not_ an intuitive method to "solve" the cube)

But it's reverse, it's *expected* that you don't have enough to understand the output. All you should see from the test cases is that's it's binary.

> The letter balance also is in no way detectable from just looking at the test cases -- this is a text representation, and differentiating between letters is quite hard when they are all mixed together; and while the first couple test cases are easy to see a difference, since same letters are grouped together, I'd say it's impossible to see how many of each letter there is for the other cases.

Agree to disagreee? The first two cases have very good spatial hints that group the letters in a way that makes the balance obvious, and if the scrambles in the later cases are too much it's always possible to use code to verify. This is reverse, some guesswork is expected.

> I'd say it is possible (even if on the harder side) to check for (…)

But that requires recognizing Rubik, which I thought you argued was unlikely.

I'm not sure we're going to agree. May I remind this puzzle has been up for like 10 years and still hasn't been auto-excluded from Reverse? (And quite a few others of mine have)

> But it's reverse, it's *expected* that you don't have enough to understand the output. 

...I don't think that's true? In reverse, the task is to figure out what the goal is. So there should be sufficient information in the (visible) tests to deduce what the goal is, otherwise it's just a guessing game. 

It is okay if deducing the goal takes time (which is exactly the measure for the ranking in reverse mode, assuming that implementing the task is easier). But one should be able to deduce it from the tests; and ideally there shouldn't be two different solutions that fit the test cases (or seem like they fit), especially if one is much easier than the other one.

> But that requires recognizing Rubik, which I thought you argued was unlikely.

I argue that it is possible for Rubik's cube to _not_ be recognized, not that it is unlikely for it to _be_ recognized. Both can be true at the same time.


> May I remind this puzzle has been up for like 10 years and still hasn't been auto-excluded from Reverse?

...doesn't mean it's a good puzzle [for reverse mode] though? May I remind you that the typo with missing spaces in the last test survived for all these years until yesterday.


> I'm not sure we're going to agree.

Yes that happens sometimes. I'm not going to force you to change it, nor will I change it myself, but I still am going to argue that it should not be set to reverse mode.
You are perfectly right. Will try to beat that... :D
